paras: The killing of George Vann was the fatal shooting of a Black man during his arrest aboard an excursion train near New Bern, North Carolina, on the night of May 4, 1903. Vann died instantly in a volley of shots as Officer C. Lupton tried to take him off the train, and a deputy, J. B. Dixon, was wounded. Wire reports said officers shot him after he resisted, while a New Bern newspaper and a coroner's jury attributed the fatal shot to persons unknown.

On the night of May 4 the Atlantic Coast Line split a Wilmington excursion of sixteen cars and about 1,000 people into two sections, citing "riotous conduct." Earlier that night Vann, described as "colored," had quarreled with Tom Green, a young white man of New Bern, and a magistrate issued a warrant for Vann. According to the New Bern Journal, the warrant charged Vann with having shot Green, and police searched for Green believing him wounded.
The Journal described Vann, also known as George Avant or "Tuck," as a former Wilmington resident recently released from the penitentiary after robbing a farmer.

Lupton, assisted by ex-policeman Breck Dixon, who had been sworn in as a deputy, boarded the train and found Vann among a group of Black companions. The Journal said Vann had boasted that it would take more than one policeman to arrest him. After a struggle, Lupton had nearly got him out of the car, the train moving about six miles an hour, when shooting broke out.

Five shots were fired by one count and eight or ten by another; Vann was struck in the mouth and killed instantly, and Dixon was shot through the thigh. When a young Black passenger moved to pull the bell cord, someone drew a pistol on him and he raised his hands. The train stopped and frightened passengers scattered, and Lupton took Vann's body off and left it beside the track.
Chief of Police Hargett, hearing the shots, ordered the conductor to go on, which the Journal said averted a possible riot.

At 2 a.m. officers found Green asleep and unhurt at his boarding house; he told them he had raised the alarm and then hidden from Vann. A coroner's jury found that Vann "came to his death at the hands of person or persons unknown who were attempting to prevent his arrest." The Journal wrote that unless someone confessed, who fired the shots, or whether the shooting was accidental, would never be known; no report of an arrest or trial was found.

The story reached readers in two forms on May 6. The Raleigh News and Observer put a New Bern special on its front page under "Bullets Hum on Excursion Train," an account the Clinton Caucasian reprinted the next day without saying who fired. A shorter wire version, carried by the Savannah Morning News as "Killed by Officers," said Vann had shot at Green, fired on Dixon and tried to throw Lupton off the train before officers killed him. The Richmond Times-Dispatch's special, headed "Ex-Convict Killed," gave the same officers' account and named a third officer, Styron.

The wire text spread through May 13 to papers in Wilmington, Delaware and South Carolina, where the Batesburg Advocate and the Manning Times printed it under the heading "Served Him Right." The Anderson Intelligencer reduced it to one line about "a desperate negro ex-convict" shot while resisting three officers.

The Wilmington Messenger then reprinted the New Bern Journal's longer account, which called Vann "a thoroughly bad man" and praised Lupton as "a brave officer" while conceding the shooter was unknown.

The wire and Richmond reports said Vann shot Dixon and that officers killed Vann. The New Bern Journal, a local account published after the inquest, said the shots came from unknown persons during an attempt by Vann's friends to block the arrest, and the coroner's verdict followed that version. Accounts also differ on the charge against Vann, from a quarrel with Green to shooting at him, though Green was later found unhurt.

reader.title: Killing of George Vann
bases: Vann was killed while a city officer and deputized assistants were arresting him on a warrant aboard an excursion train (A1, A4, A6); no mob or crowd acted against him.

Independent New Bern dispatches to Richmond (A1), Raleigh (A3, A4) and the wire (A2), and the New Bern Journal account (A6), agree that Vann was shot dead during the arrest and that Dixon was wounded, though they disagree on who fired.

accounts.label: Wire and Richmond special (officers' version)
accounts.gist: Vann resisted three officers, shot Dixon in the thigh and tried to throw Lupton off the train; a fusillade followed and the officers killed him.

accounts.label: Raleigh special
accounts.gist: After a quarrel with Green led to a warrant, Lupton arrested Vann, who grabbed the officer on the platform; five shots were fired, killing Vann and wounding Dixon, without saying who fired.

accounts.label: New Bern Journal and coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Vann's friends tried to prevent the arrest; eight or ten shots were fired by persons unknown, and the coroner's jury so found; whether the shooting was accidental could not be known.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Ex-Convict Killed' and 'Negro Put Up a Fight and a Shot Ended His Career' cast Vann as a resisting criminal and the officers as acting lawfully.
The New Bern Journal called Vann 'a thoroughly bad man' and said Lupton 'deserves much credit' for arresting 'a dangerous criminal.'
Two South Carolina weeklies ran the wire text under the heading 'Served Him Right.'
A Delaware paper and the Anderson Intelligencer carried the wire version as a brief news item.

info: Monday night, May 4, 1903, about 11:30 p.m. (dispatches dated May 5 say 'last night')
Aboard the Atlantic Coast Line excursion train bound for Wilmington, as it had almost reached the New Bern city limits, moving about six miles an hour
George Vann (also 'George Van', alias George Avant, alias 'Tuck'), described as 'colored' and a 'negro ex-convict'
Accused of shooting at, or shooting, Tom (Thomas) Green, a young white man, earlier that night; one dispatch says only that the two quarreled. Green was later found unhurt.

Contested: the wire says Vann was shot to death 'by officers' (Lupton, Dixon and a third officer); the New Bern Journal says he was killed 'by some unknow person' and the coroner's jury blamed persons unknown attempting to prevent his arrest.
Lupton took the body off the train and left it beside the track; the chief ordered the train on. No report of an arrest, indictment or trial was found.
